answer.summary: Base editing (Komor 2016 CBE; Gaudelli 2017 ABE; Nishida 2016 Target-AID) chemically interconverts base pairs at a nicked locus — efficient and donor-free, but limited to transitions and burdened by bystander edits plus guide-independent deaminase off-target activity on DNA (Zuo 2019) and RNA (Gruenewald 2019). Prime editing (Anzalone 2019) writes arbitrary short sequences via a reverse transcriptase and pegRNA, covering all 12 substitutions and small indels with much lower bystander risk, but with a larger three-component cargo and historically lower in vivo efficiency. The 2021-2026 engineering arc closed much of that gap: PE4/PE5/PEmax (Chen 2021) overcame mismatch-repair suppression, epegRNAs (Nelson 2021) stabilized guides, PE6 (Doman 2023) shrank the editor for viral packaging, and ABE8e (Richter 2020) supplied the fast deaminase used clinically. Delivery splits three ways — LNP mRNA for liver (Musunuru 2021, Rothgangl 2021, Jiang 2026), dual-AAV for brain/liver/heart (Davis 2023), and engineered virus-like particles delivering transient RNPs with near-undetectable off-target editing (Banskota 2022; An 2024 for prime editors). Evidence is sharply stratified. Preclinical animal work is mature: lifespan extension in progeria mice (Koblan 2021), PKU correction in mice (Boeck 2022), SCD correction in patient HSPCs engrafted in mice (Newby 2021, Everette 2023), and durable ~60% LDL reduction in macaques. Human evidence is narrower: base editing has four published clinical reports — ex vivo CAR7 T cells (6 patients), ex vivo risto-cel for sickle cell disease (31 patients, the largest cohort), one bespoke n-of-1 in vivo LNP therapy for CPS1 deficiency, and the 35-patient VERVE-102 in vivo dose-ranging trial. Prime editing has exactly one clinical report, PM359 in two patients, ex vivo only; no in vivo prime editing has reached humans.
gaps: Eight papers have empty quotes because OpenAlex returned null abstracts (Komor 2016, Gaudelli 2017, Anzalone 2019, Richter 2020, Nelson 2021, Gruenewald 2019, Newby 2021, Koblan 2021) — including three of the four foundational papers. No invented quotes were substituted.

Citation edges are inferential, not reference-list-verified: the Semantic Scholar/OpenAlex outage removed access to bibliographies, so the four reported edges rest on the citing abstract explicitly naming the prior system (PE2/PE3, PEmax, 'our previously reported base editor eVLP architecture'). Many real edges among these papers are therefore unreported.

Two quotes are not author-written abstract text: Zuo 2019's is the Science editors' summary occupying the indexed abstract field, and Musunuru 2021's is a short full-text fragment recovered by web search after the abstract proved unretrievable.

No peer-reviewed in vivo prime editing in non-human primates exists in the literature found; the only NHP prime-editing liver data (GSD1b, ~50% editing at day 14) is a company press release with no durability readout.

Human durability and long-term safety data are absent beyond roughly 18 months (VERVE-102) and 6 months (PM359); no published human data address whether the deaminase-independent off-target mutagenesis seen in embryos and cell lines occurs at clinical doses.

Cut at the 25-paper ceiling though verified and relevant: Villiger 2018 (first in vivo base editing of a metabolic disease), Levy 2020 (AAV base editing across five tissues), Breda 2023 (in vivo CD117-targeted LNP HSC editing), Koblan 2018 (BE4max/ABEmax), Anzalone 2021 (twin prime editing for large sequence replacement), Mathis 2024 (PRIDICT2.0 efficiency prediction), and Hanna 2026 (Cas12a reni-cel, a same-indication double-strand-break comparator to risto-cel).

Immunogenicity is an underexplored risk: Rothgangl 2021 reports a humoral response to the editor that blocked redosing in macaques, but no clinical paper in this list reports anti-editor immunity data in humans.
Coverage is skewed toward liver and haematopoietic targets; delivery to muscle, kidney, lung and the CNS in large animals is not represented by any paper found.

answer.summary:
Base editing and prime editing are the two principal DSB-free alternatives to nuclease genome editing. Base editors (Komor 2016 for C-to-T; Gaudelli 2017 for A-to-G) fuse a deaminase to a Cas9 nickase and perform a direct chemical conversion at a target base: very efficient, minimal indels, but limited to transition mutations inside a narrow editing window. Prime editing (Anzalone 2019) fuses a nickase to a reverse transcriptase programmed by a pegRNA, covering all 12 point mutations plus small insertions and deletions, at the cost of lower efficiency, a larger cargo, and dependence on mismatch repair — addressed by PE4/PE5/PEmax (Chen 2021), epegRNAs (Nelson 2021) and the compact PE6 editors (Doman 2023). Engineering follow-ups (BE4max/ABEmax, ABE8e) raised both classes to therapeutic activity levels.

Delivery divides by tissue and by cargo persistence. LNPs carrying editor mRNA plus guide RNA dominate liver targets, inheriting the biodegradable-LNP/modified-sgRNA platform from Finn 2018, validated in macaques by Musunuru 2021 and Rothgangl 2021 and now in humans. Engineered virus-like particles (Banskota 2022) deliver transient ribonucleoprotein with near-undetectable off-target editing and reach the retina; they were extended to prime editors by An 2024 and improved again by Geilenkeuser 2025. Dual-AAV (Davis 2023) reaches brain, liver and heart but gives persistent expression. Prime editing trailed base editing in delivery by roughly three years because of editor size.

The preclinical/clinical boundary is sharp. Progeria, phenylketonuria, genetic blindness, Angptl3 and all in vivo prime editing in brain/liver/heart remain mouse or macaque evidence only. Human evidence exists in five places: base-edited CAR7 T cells (Chiesa 2023), ex vivo base-edited HSPCs for sickle cell disease (risto-cel, NEJM 2026), in vivo LNP base editing of PCSK9 in 35 patients (VERVE-102, NEJM 2026), a bespoke n-of-1 in vivo therapy for CPS1 deficiency (Musunuru 2025), and the only prime-editing clinical data anywhere — PM359 in two patients with p47-phox CGD (NEJM 2025), which is ex vivo rather than in vivo.
gaps: No in vivo prime editing has entered human trials; PM359 is ex vivo HSPC editing, leaving the gap between Davis 2023 mouse brain/liver/heart AAV delivery and any clinical in vivo prime editor unbridged.
Engineered virus-like particles have no clinical data at all — all evidence is mouse retina and liver.
Longest human follow-up for in vivo base editing is about one year (VERVE-102); durability claims rest on macaque data. PM359 follow-up is 4-6 months in only two patients.
Re-dosing is blocked by anti-editor humoral immunity, observed in macaques by Rothgangl 2021, with no published clinical solution.
Off-target assessment in humans is indirect; unbiased genome-wide methods such as CHANGE-seq-BE are applied preclinically while clinical trials report surrogate safety endpoints.
Extrahepatic LNP targeting is largely unsolved outside GalNAc-mediated liver tropism; there is no clinical LNP editing outside the liver.

C-to-G transversion editors (CGBE1; Zhao 2021) lack in vivo therapeutic validation, and a 2024 Nature Cell Biology report that C-to-G editing generates double-strand breaks undercuts the DSB-free premise for that editor class specifically.

OpenAlex was budget-exhausted and Semantic Scholar timed out on all forward-citation lookups, so 2025-2026 forward-citation coverage is incomplete and recent delivery-engineering preprints may be missing.
Citation edges reported here derive only from backward reference-list evidence; no forward-citation edges could be verified.

answer.summary: Base editing and prime editing both avoid the double-strand breaks that make nuclease editing imprecise (indels, translocations, chromothripsis, p53 activation), but they trade off differently. Base editors (Komor 2016 for C-to-T; Gaudelli 2017 for A-to-G) are chemically simple, highly efficient in vivo (60-90% liver editing), and restricted to transition substitutions plus bystander-edit and Cas-independent deamination risks. Prime editors (Anzalone 2019) install any substitution and small indels using a pegRNA-templated reverse transcription, with far lower off-target activity but lower and more sequence-dependent efficiency; most subsequent work (PE4/PE5 MMR evasion, epegRNAs, PE6, PE7/La) exists to close that efficiency gap. Delivery splits three ways: LNP-mRNA (transient, redosable, liver-restricted, and the vehicle for all human in vivo data), dual AAV (broad tropism including brain and heart, but persistent editor expression), and engineered VLPs (transient RNP, viral tropism, best demonstrated in retina). The evidence hierarchy is clearly asymmetric. Preclinical animal evidence is rich for both modalities: progeria rescue, PKU correction by both base and prime editing, NHP PCSK9 knockdown, retinal prime editing by eVLP, and 2025-2026 LNP prime editing reaching ~49% mouse liver editing. Human evidence is base editing only and still thin: ex vivo base-edited CAR7 T cells (Chiesa 2023) and a single bespoke in vivo LNP base-editing case for CPS1 deficiency (Musunuru 2025). Published human prime editing is ex vivo and limited to two CGD patients; there is no peer-reviewed in vivo human prime editing at all. The most widely cited current clinical numbers (VERVE-102, BEAM-101, BEAM-302) come from company press releases, not journals.
gaps: No peer-reviewed publication located for the Verve VERVE-101/VERVE-102 PCSK9 trials (Heart-1, Heart-2); all efficacy and safety figures circulating are company interim press releases from an open-label, single-arm dose-escalation design.

No peer-reviewed publication located for Beam's BEAM-101 (sickle cell, ex vivo) or BEAM-302 (alpha-1 antitrypsin, in vivo LNP) trials, despite BEAM-302 being described as the first clinical correction of a disease-causing mutation.

Press coverage indicates an NEJM paper on PM359 prime-edited HSCs for chronic granulomatous disease (December 2025, two patients) exists, but I could not verify its exact title, authors or DOI within the tool budget; it is the only published human prime editing and is absent from the list for that reason.
No published human in vivo prime editing of any kind; the modality's clinical evidence is entirely ex vivo.
Durability and cellular distribution of in vivo edits in humans are unresolved: the CPS1 case had no liver biopsy, leaving editing mosaicism and long-term persistence unmeasured.

Delivery remains narrow in practice: LNP work is overwhelmingly hepatocyte-targeted, eVLP in vivo success is largely retinal, and extrahepatic/extraocular non-viral delivery has little therapeutic-grade evidence.

Long-term off-target and immunogenicity surveillance in treated humans (anti-Cas9/anti-deaminase immunity, LNP redosing immunogenicity, RNA off-target deamination) is not covered by any paper in this list.

Head-to-head comparisons of base vs prime vs nuclease editing on the same target in the same in vivo model are rare, so the efficiency/precision tradeoff is inferred across studies rather than measured directly.
Economics and regulatory pathway for n-of-1 bespoke editors, raised by the CPS1 case, have no peer-reviewed evidence base yet.

answer.summary:
Three DSB-free editing modalities now span bench to bedside. Cytosine base editors (Komor 2016; Nishida 2016) and adenine base editors (Gaudelli 2017, accelerated by ABE8e in Richter 2020) make single transition substitutions with high efficiency and low indel rates, but cannot perform arbitrary edits and carry a distinctive guide-independent deaminase off-target risk (Zuo 2019) absent from Cas9 nuclease editing. Prime editing (Anzalone 2019) trades efficiency for generality — all 12 substitutions plus small indels — and its history since is largely about recovering that efficiency and purity: MMR evasion via MLH1dn (Chen 2021), pegRNA stabilization (Nelson 2022), compact evolved RTs for delivery (Doman 2023), La-domain fusion (Yan 2024), and nick-degradation engineering to cut indel byproducts up to 60-fold (Chauhan 2025).

Delivery separates the two clinically. LNP-formulated mRNA plus gRNA reaches hepatocytes transiently and is the only route with substantial in vivo human data; AAV (split-intein dual vectors, Levy 2020; dual-AAV prime editors, Davis 2024) reaches brain, retina, heart and muscle but persists as DNA; eVLPs (Banskota 2022; An 2024) deliver editor RNPs transiently and reached therapeutic retinal editing in mice, but remain entirely preclinical.

The preclinical/clinical boundary is sharp. Preclinical animal evidence: PCSK9 knockdown in macaques (Musunuru 2021; Rothgangl 2021; Lee 2023), lifespan extension in progeria mice (Koblan 2021), sickle allele correction in patient HSPCs engrafted in mice by base editing (Newby 2021) and prime editing (Everette 2023), and eVLP/AAV editing of CNS and retina. Human clinical evidence is still narrow: ex vivo multiplex CBE in CAR7 T cells (Chiesa 2023), one N-of-1 in vivo ABE infusion for CPS1 deficiency (Musunuru 2025), ex vivo prime-edited CD34+ cells in two CGD participants (Gori 2026), and the largest dataset — 35 adults given VERVE-102, with PCSK9 down up to 88% and LDL-C up to ~62% at a median ~9 months (Vafai 2026). No in vivo prime editing has been reported in humans, and no DSB-free editor has completed a randomized controlled trial.

Caveat on provenance: I directly verified the NEJM 2025/2026 records, the PE7 and vPE Nature records, and the prime-editor eVLP record this session. Other DOIs are from recall and are worth a one-click check before citation.
gaps: No in vivo prime editing has been reported in humans; all clinical prime editing to date is ex vivo autologous HSC therapy in two participants, so the modality with the broadest editing scope has the thinnest human safety record.
Engineered virus-like particles have no clinical data at all. The gap between mouse retina/CNS results and any first-in-human eVLP trial is the largest unbridged translation step in the field.

Long-term durability and oncogenic risk are unestablished. The longest human follow-up here is ~18 months in a 35-patient open-label phase 1; no randomized controlled trial, no clinical-endpoint data (e.g. cardiovascular events), and no multi-year surveillance for edited-clone expansion.

Guide-independent deaminase off-target mutagenesis (Zuo 2019) is well characterized in mouse embryos and cell lines, but there is no published method for measuring it directly in treated human tissue; clinical off-target assessment relies on in vitro surrogates such as HuH-7 cells and primary hepatocytes.

Delivery is still essentially liver-only for in vivo clinical work. LNP tropism to hematopoietic stem cells, muscle and CNS is active preclinical work (CD117-targeted LNPs, bone-marrow-homing LNPs, in utero delivery) but I found no peer-reviewed in vivo human results outside hepatocytes.

Head-to-head comparisons are missing: no study in my list directly benchmarks base editing versus prime editing versus HDR/nuclease editing on the same target, delivery vehicle and animal model, so relative efficiency/purity claims are cross-study inferences.

N-of-1 regulatory and manufacturing precedent rests on a single patient; there is no published framework or outcome series establishing whether bespoke base editors are reproducible or scalable across patients.

I could not confirm a peer-reviewed publication for BEAM-101 (base-edited HSCs for sickle cell disease) despite multiple conference datasets through ASH 2025 — that evidence remains in press releases and abstracts, not the literature.

Some 2025 preclinical results I am aware of but could not verify well enough to list (in vivo prime editing for alternating hemiplegia of childhood in mice, Cell 2025; base editing extending lifespan in a humanized prion disease mouse model, Nature Medicine 2025) would strengthen the CNS preclinical picture if confirmed.

Several DOIs in this list were drawn from memory rather than verified this session (Richter 2020, Nelson 2022, Doman 2023, Levy 2020, Rothgangl 2021, Everette 2023, Davis 2024, Lee 2023) and should be checked; likewise, quotes were left empty wherever I could not confirm verbatim abstract wording.

answer.summary:
The literature splits into two problems that use different tools.

(1) Global rotation (deskew) estimates a single angle for a scanned page. The classical approaches are projection profiles, the Hough transform and Fourier-spectrum methods. Pal & Chaudhuri (1996) and the Fast Hough Transform detector of Bezmaternykh & Nikolaev are examples. The current Fourier method is Pham et al.'s Adaptive Radial Projection, which projects the 2D DFT magnitude spectrum along radial lines and also contributes the DISE-2021 dataset. Evaluation is standardized by the ICDAR 2013 DISEC contest, which uses the AED, TOP80 and CE measures.

(2) Single-image dewarping corrects curved, folded or perspective-distorted camera-captured pages, which needs a dense non-rigid mapping. Model-based approaches came first (Liang et al., TPAMI 2008). DocUNet (CVPR 2018) then introduced learned backward-map regression along with the DocUNet benchmark. DewarpNet/Doc3D (2019) added explicit 3D-shape supervision. Later work changed how the mapping is represented: dense flow (FCN displacement, patch-based CNN), transformer displacement (DocTr, DocTr++), geometric priors from 3D shape plus text lines (DocGeoNet, D2Dewarp, grid regularization), sparse control points or TPS (Document Dewarping with Control Points, FDRNet, which also uses Fourier high-frequency cues), and 3D/2D grid meshes (UVDoc).

From 2024 to 2026 the trends are generalist restoration models (DocRes), generative or diffusion mapping (DvD), progressive dewarping (TADoc), and explicit global-then-local cascades (Cascaded Robust Rectification). That last work handles global affine/perspective correction first and curved-paper correction second, which joins the two problems in one pipeline. Evaluation work is growing as well: new benchmarks (UVDoc, Inv3D, AnyPhotoDoc6300) and new metrics (AAD, DLS) that go beyond MS-SSIM, Local Distortion, CER and ED on DocUNet.

Citation evidence: the edges come from Citation Lens reference lists, mostly arXiv primary bibliographies for UVDoc and Semantic Scholar index edges. No citation edges were found between the deskew papers and the dewarping papers; the two groups appear largely separate.
gaps: OpenAlex was over its daily budget and Semantic Scholar timed out on several queries, so forward-citation coverage is incomplete. In particular, DocUNet's citing papers and references could not be retrieved directly.

The DOI for the DISEC 2013 contest report was not verified. The DOI I guessed, 10.1109/ICDAR.2013.293, resolved to a different ICDAR 2013 competition and was dropped. The paper's existence is supported by DBLP and by its use in arXiv:1912.02504, but I had no verbatim abstract to quote. The DBLP link given is a search-result author page, not the paper record.

Classical Fourier deskew foundations, such as Postl (1986) and Baird's work on projection profiles, were not retrieved. Pal & Chaudhuri (1996) and Liang et al. (2008) had no abstract in the index, so their quotes are empty.
Learned global-rotation work was not covered: CNN skew regression and 0/90/180/270 page-orientation classification.
Edges from 1912.02504 to DISEC and among the skew papers were not checked against reference lists, so no deskew citation edges are reported.

No classical model-based curved-page methods beyond Liang et al. 2008 were verified, e.g. text-line or shape-from-shading methods and Metric Rectification of Curved Document Images (TPAMI 2012), which appeared in the graph but was not read.
No dedicated survey or meta-evaluation of dewarping metrics was found. Evaluation evidence comes from benchmark and metric contributions inside method papers (DocUNet, UVDoc, Inv3D, DvD, AAD, TADoc).

answer.summary:
The two problems are solved differently.

**Global rotation (deskew)** is a single-parameter problem. The page is flat and only rotated, so classical methods find the dominant text-line orientation in one pass. The Fourier approach (Pham et al., adaptive radial projection on the DFT magnitude spectrum) and Hough-transform approaches (Bezmaternykh & Nikolaev's fast Hough transform) are both projection-family methods. They are fast, need no training data, and are benchmarked on DISEC'13 and DISE-2021 using AED, TOP80 and CE.

**Curved-page dewarping** has to estimate a dense, non-rigid warp. The literature moved through several stages:
- **Direct dense mapping:** DocUNet's stacked U-Net predicting a forward map.
- **3D-shape-aware regression:** DewarpNet and its Doc3D dataset.
- **Displacement-flow regressors:** the FCN flow method, then transformer models (DocTr, DocTr++) and recurrent refinement (DocScanner).
- **Sparse control-point and grid parameterizations:** control points, DocReal and UVDoc's 3D/2D grid.
- **Geometry and text-line priors:** DocGeoNet, RDGR's grid-regularized optimization, D2Dewarp and ForCenNet.
- **Frequency-domain cues:** FDRNet, which bridges the Fourier idea from deskewing into learned TPS dewarping.
- **Generative mapping (newest):** DvD's coordinate-level diffusion.

Recent work also makes the overlap between the two problems explicit: Axis-Aligned Dewarping adds an axis-alignment pre-processing step, and TADoc handles rotated as well as curved inputs.

**Evaluation is a research topic in its own right.** The DocUNet benchmark (MS-SSIM, LD, plus OCR error rates) is the default. PaperEdge showed flaws in MS-SSIM and LD and proposed Aligned Distortion; UVDoc adds a line-straightness metric; DocMatcher proposes mnCER; Axis-Aligned Dewarping proposes AAD. Newer real-image benchmarks include DIR300, UVDoc, Inv3D, AnyPhotoDoc6300 and DocReal's Chinese set, and Document Registration offers automatic labeling of real photo pairs.

**How the citation links were found:** Semantic Scholar timed out and OpenAlex had hit its daily budget. The links therefore come from Citation Lens's citation-index edges and from UVDoc's arXiv reference list, which was checked directly. DocTr and FDRNet are the most-cited hubs among the papers selected.
gaps: Semantic Scholar timed out and OpenAlex had exhausted its daily budget, so forward-citation coverage is incomplete. Missing citation edges, especially for the deskew papers and for DocUNet and DewarpNet, do not mean those citations don't exist.

No verified DOI or URL was found for the original contest papers: the ICDAR 2013 Document Image Skew Estimation Contest (DISEC'13; Papandreou et al., pp. 1444–1448) and the CBDAR 2007 Document Image Dewarping Contest (Shafait & Breuel; PDF at dfki.de). Both are left out of the list even though they are the main evaluation foundations for each subproblem.

Classical deskew foundations (Postl's 1986 Fourier/projection method, Baird's projection profiles, Hough-based methods, Fabrizio's ICIP 2014 Fourier method that won DISEC'13) and classical model-based dewarping (shape-from-shading, cylinder models, text-line fitting) are not represented by verified records.
No deep-learning paper on rotation or skew regression was found within the call budget, so learned global-rotation methods are under-covered.
No recent survey (2024–2026) of document dewarping was found. The 2021 survey by Wagdy et al. in the International Journal of Image and Graphics was seen but not verified.
The arXiv posting of Pham et al. is dated 2026, but the work is from ICIP 2022, so it should be cited as the 2022 conference paper.

answer.summary:
I found 24 papers, but only some could be checked against their pages within the 8-call budget. I checked UVDoc, DvD and D2Dewarp directly. DocMatcher, TADoc, ForCenNet, Polar-Doc, Marior, RDGR, DocTr++, the 2025 evaluation-metric paper and the Fast Hough deskew paper turned up in search results with their URLs. Every non-empty quote comes from a search snippet, not a checked abstract, and some abstracts may be cut off. The arXiv IDs for DocTr, DocGeoNet, DocScanner, FDRNet and DocRes, and the DOIs for PaperEdge and docstrum, are from memory, not checked. The four classic skew papers (Postl, DISEC'13, Fabrizio) point to dblp search pages, because I couldn't confirm their exact DOIs; the Fabrizio page at EPITA returned 404.

**Global rotation (deskewing) and curved-page correction (dewarping) are separate problems.**

- **Deskewing** finds one in-plane angle, usually needed to within about 0.1–0.2°. The classic methods rely on regular text lines:
  - Fourier or power-spectrum and projection-profile methods (Postl 1986).
  - Nearest-neighbour angle statistics, called docstrum (O'Gorman 1993).
  - Hough-transform voting (the Fast Hough paper).
  - Hybrids such as Fabrizio's KNN clustering plus Fourier, which later work reports as the top method at DISEC'13.
- **Deskew evaluation** centres on DISEC'13: 155 base images rotated within ±15°, scored by average error (AED), the top-80% error (TOP80) and the share of estimates within 0.1° (CE). DISE-2021 builds on it.
- **Dewarping** has to undo a non-rigid 3D page shape, so a single angle is not enough. The field moved to learned dense geometric mappings:
  - Stacked U-Net flow regression (DocUNet).
  - 3D-shape then backward-map regression trained on the synthetic Doc3D set (DewarpNet).
  - Transformer flow regression (DocTr and DocTr++).
  - Shape and text-line priors (DocGeoNet, RDGR, D2Dewarp).
  - Iterative refinement (DocScanner) and margin handling (Marior).
  - Grid and mesh outputs (UVDoc).
  - Weak supervision from real photos (PaperEdge).
  - Diffusion over coordinates (DvD) and foreground- or time-aware variants (ForCenNet, TADoc).
- **The Fourier idea carries over.** FDRNet learns rectification from structure-preserving low-frequency Fourier components.
- **Dewarping benchmarks** include DocUNet (130 images), DIR300, DocReal, UVDoc and the new AnyPhotoDoc6300 from DvD. Several papers find the usual metrics flawed:
  - MS-SSIM and LD (local distortion) react to small shifts and scale changes.
  - Scores depend on the evaluation environment (Polar-Doc reports Matlab sensitivity).
  - OCR error rates often disagree with image metrics.
  - Proposed fixes include AD (aligned distortion), mnCER (DocMatcher), DLS (TADoc) and an alignment-based metric (DD, 2025).

**Citation links.** Links from D2Dewarp to earlier work come from its reference list. The UVDoc and DvD links come from their abstracts, which name the DocUNet benchmark, the Doc3D set and the DIR300 set they evaluate on. DewarpNet citing DocUNet, DocTr++ citing DocTr, and the Fast Hough paper citing DISEC'13 are strong inferences from how those papers build on or evaluate against that work, not checked reference lists.
gaps: I found no learned global-deskew paper from 2024–2026 with a confirmed abstract. Deep skew estimators (e.g., DISE-2021 related work, neural-deskew) were found only as datasets or code repos.
The DISEC'13 contest report, Postl 1986 and Fabrizio ICIP 2014 are linked through dblp search pages rather than checked DOIs. Their quotes are left empty.
Baird's 1987 projection-profile paper and Hull's 1998 survey of skew-detection methods were not included because their sources could not be checked within budget.
Several arXiv IDs and DOIs (DocTr, DocGeoNet, DocScanner, FDRNet, DocRes, PaperEdge, docstrum) come from prior knowledge and were not checked in this session.
Citation links are limited to those backed by evidence (mainly D2Dewarp's reference list). Many real citation links among DocTr, DocGeoNet, DocScanner, UVDoc and the 2025 methods are left out.
Classical non-learned dewarping methods (3D reconstruction from shading or stereo, text-line spline and cylinder models, the CBDAR 2007 dewarping contest) are not covered.
There is no cross-benchmark comparison of deskew accuracy against dewarping pipelines on rotated-and-curved pages. No work joining the two problems was found.

answer.summary:
I made all 8 allowed tool calls. All citation links come from reference lists I checked directly: the jdeskew paper (arXiv 2603.05942), D2Dewarp and UVDoc, plus FDRNet's citation of DewarpNet. Papers that only evaluate on a benchmark (DvD, ForCenNet, DocMamba) get no link unless I saw the reference itself.

**Global rotation versus curved pages.** Deskewing estimates a single rotation angle, while dewarping estimates a dense non-rigid mapping.

**Deskewing (one global angle).** The classical families are:
- projection profiles and their Fourier/Radon versions, starting with Postl (1986);
- Hough transforms (Srihari & Govindaraju, 1989);
- the families catalogued in Hull's 1998 survey.

DISEC 2013 is the standard benchmark. Fourier-domain methods still lead in practice:
- Fabrizio (2014) clusters regions and then applies a Fourier transform; the authors' lab says it ranked first at DISEC'13.
- Pham et al. (jdeskew; ICIP 2022, on arXiv in 2026) use adaptive radial projection on the DFT magnitude spectrum and add the DISE-2021 dataset.

**Dewarping (curved, folded or wrinkled pages).**
- Classical single-image methods fit 3D surfaces or optimize text-line straightness (Tian & Narasimhan 2011; Kim et al. 2015).
- Learned methods began with DocUNet (2018, which also gave the 130-image benchmark) and DewarpNet (2019, 3D shape prior plus the Doc3D training set). These established direct regression of a backward map.
- Later work added transformers (DocTr, DocTr++), geometric cues such as 3D shape and text lines (DocGeoNet, which brought the DIR300 benchmark), regularization (RDGR), weak supervision from real photos (PaperEdge), and coarse grids (UVDoc).
- FDRNet links the two areas: it works on high-frequency Fourier components and a Thin-Plate Spline warp, and released the WarpDoc dataset.

**Last two years (Oct 2024 – Oct 2026).** Work has shifted to:
- generative coordinate diffusion (DvD, with the 6,300-pair AnyPhotoDoc6300 benchmark);
- state-space models (DocMamba);
- dual-direction line geometry (D2Dewarp);
- foreground-centric rectification (ForCenNet);
- cascaded rectification of arbitrary documents (Cascaded Robust Rectification, Nov 2025).

Evaluation still mostly uses DocUNet and DIR300 with MS-SSIM, LD (local distortion), CER and ED (OCR error rates).
gaps: Only 2 of the 25 papers have verified abstract quotes (UVDoc, D2Dewarp). The fetch tool would not return longer verbatim abstracts, so every other quote field is empty.

DISEC 2013, Postl 1986, Hull 1998, Srihari & Govindaraju 1989, Tian & Narasimhan 2011, Kim et al. 2015, PaperEdge and RDGR have Google Scholar query URLs as placeholders. The budget ran out before I could confirm their DOIs or arXiv IDs. PaperEdge and RDGR are not in any search result; I confirmed them only from entries in the UVDoc and D2Dewarp reference lists.
Baird's 1987 projection-profile skew paper and O'Gorman's docstrum are well-known foundational works, but I could not verify them within the budget, so they are not on the list.
I found no deep-learning global-skew estimator or recent (2024–2026) skew benchmark beyond DISE-2021. Learned deskewing looks under-studied, or at least under-indexed.
The search found no dedicated dewarping evaluation-metric or survey paper, such as the CBDAR 2007 dewarping contest or a 2024–25 rectification survey. UVDoc does not cite the CBDAR 2007 contest.
Benchmark comparability is poor. Papers use different DocUNet and DIR300 subsets (for example, 50/60 or 90 text-rich images for OCR), and some re-train baselines on their own data.
For DvD, ForCenNet and DocMamba I did not open the reference lists, so their outgoing citation links are left out. I saw only that they report results on DocUNet and DIR300.

papers.title: FlashAttention: Fast and Memory-Efficient Exact Attention with IO-Awareness
papers.role: Foundational GPU I/O-aware exact attention kernel
papers.reason: Defines the tiling-plus-recomputation IO-aware kernel that every later paper here builds on; all 13 seeds I expanded cite it.
papers.quote: We propose FlashAttention, an IO-aware exact attention algorithm that uses tiling to reduce the number of memory reads/writes between GPU high bandwidth memory (HBM) and GPU on-chip SRAM.

papers.title: Self-attention Does Not Need $O(n^2)$ Memory
papers.reason: Shows exact attention can run in O(1)/O(log n) memory using chunked, incrementally normalized softmax; FlashAttention-2, Ring Attention and others cite it.
papers.quote: We present a very simple algorithm for attention that requires $O(1)$ memory with respect to sequence length and an extension to self-attention that requires $O(\log n)$ memory.

papers.title: Online normalizer calculation for softmax
papers.reason: The single-pass running max/normalizer trick that makes tiled exact attention possible.
papers.quote: In this paper we propose a way to compute classical Softmax with fewer memory accesses and hypothesize that this reduction in memory accesses should improve Softmax performance on actual hardware.

papers.title: FlashAttention-2: Faster Attention with Better Parallelism and Work Partitioning
papers.role: Influential follow-up: parallelism and work partitioning inside the kernel
papers.reason: Changes how work is split across thread blocks and warps to fix low occupancy; now the standard exact kernel.
papers.quote: We observe that the inefficiency is due to suboptimal work partitioning between different thread blocks and warps on the GPU, causing either low-occupancy or unnecessary shared memory reads/writes.

papers.title: FlashAttention-3: Fast and Accurate Attention with Asynchrony and Low-precision
papers.role: Hopper-generation I/O-aware kernel (counted for its exact FP16 path only)
papers.reason: Uses warp specialization and overlaps matmul with softmax for exact FP16 attention on H100. Its FP8 path is excluded as low-precision.
papers.quote: exploiting asynchrony of the Tensor Cores and TMA to (1) overlap overall computation and data movement via warp-specialization and (2) interleave block-wise matmul and softmax operations

papers.title: Ring Attention with Blockwise Transformers for Near-Infinite Context
papers.role: Foundational distributed exact attention (ring / context parallelism)
papers.reason: Splits the sequence across devices and overlaps the passing of KV blocks around a ring with blockwise attention compute, with no approximation.
papers.quote: Our approach enables training and inference of sequences that are up to device count times longer than those achievable by prior memory-efficient Transformers, without resorting to approximations

papers.title: Blockwise Parallel Transformer for Large Context Models
papers.role: Memory algorithm on a single device: blockwise attention fused with the feedforward network
papers.reason: Extends blockwise exact attention to the FFN on one device; Ring Attention is built on top of it.
papers.quote: We present a distinct approach, Blockwise Parallel Transformer (BPT), that leverages blockwise computation of self-attention and feedforward network fusion to minimize memory costs.

papers.title: Sequence Parallelism: Long Sequence Training from System Perspective
papers.reason: First to split the sequence across GPUs and compute attention with ring-style communication.
papers.quote: we propose sequence parallelism, a memory-efficient parallelism to solve this issue from system perspective instead.

papers.title: DeepSpeed Ulysses: System Optimizations for Enabling Training of Extreme Long Sequence Transformer Models
papers.reason: The main alternative to ring-based approaches: all-to-all exchanges re-partition the sequence across attention heads.

papers.quote: We propose three key techniques: token-level workload balancing, overlapping key-value communication, and a rematerialization-aware gradient checkpointing algorithm.

answer.summary:
I found 25 papers in four groups.

**Foundational memory algorithms.** Online softmax (Milakov & Gimelshein 2018) keeps a running max and normalizer so softmax can be computed in one streaming pass. Chen et al. (2016) introduced trading extra compute for memory through recomputation. Rabe & Staats (2021) combined these ideas into chunked exact attention needing O(1) or O(log n) memory.

**GPU I/O-aware kernels.** FlashAttention (2022) turned this into an exact kernel that tiles work in on-chip SRAM to cut reads and writes to GPU memory (HBM); it is cited by every seed I expanded. FlashAttention-2 fixed how work is split across thread blocks and warps. FlashAttention-3 uses asynchronous hardware features on Hopper GPUs. Lean Attention and FlashInfer focus on load balancing during decoding. FlexAttention, FlashMask and ThunderKittens (2024–25) make exact fused kernels easier to write: through a compiler, a sparse mask format and tile abstractions, respectively.

**Distributed attention.** These papers fall into two families:
- **Ring / context parallelism:** each device passes key-value blocks to its neighbour while computing. Examples: Li et al.'s Ring Self-Attention, Ring Attention with Blockwise Parallel Transformer, Striped Attention (balances causal workloads), DistFlashAttn, BurstAttention, TokenRing, and the pass-KV/pass-Q inference variants for million-token contexts.
- **Head-parallel all-to-all:** DeepSpeed Ulysses.

Several papers combine or extend these. USP and LoongTrain mix both families; Mesh-Attention assigns each GPU a 2D tile to cut communication; Tree Attention uses a tree reduction for decoding; Untied Ulysses (UPipe) chunks attention by head to cut memory.

**Main trade-offs.**
- Ring methods scale past the number of attention heads but send more data per GPU.
- Ulysses communicates efficiently but is capped by the number of heads.
- 2D and mesh methods try to get both benefits.
- Within one GPU, the gains shift from memory savings (FlashAttention v1) to keeping the hardware busy (v2/v3) and to programmability (Flex, ThunderKittens).

**Citation links.** The citation links come from reference-list data the citation tool returned. They are not complete, because Semantic Scholar and OpenAlex timed out or ran out of quota during the search.
gaps: Excluded by scope, covered only here: approximate or sparse attention (Reformer, Linformer, Performer, Longformer, BigBird, MInference, StreamingLLM); low-precision kernels (FlashAttention-3's FP8 path, 4-bit or quantized FlashAttention variants such as HiFA4 and QFlash); and KV-cache serving policies (PagedAttention/vLLM, LoongServe, eviction and compression). FlashDecoding++ was left out because it replaces the online-softmax max with a unified value that falls back on overflow, so its exactness depends on that fallback. FlashInfer is included only for its kernels.

Provider coverage was poor: Semantic Scholar timed out and OpenAlex's daily quota was used up during the search, so discovery relied mostly on arXiv. Forward citations, and therefore the newest follow-ups such as a possible FlashAttention-4 or Blackwell-specific kernels, were not checked directly.

Citation links come only from reference lists the citation tool returned. Some pairs that probably exist (for example DeepSpeed Ulysses and Blockwise Parallel Transformer to earlier work, or ThunderKittens to FlashAttention) were not confirmed and are left out. The FlashAttention -> Self-attention Does Not Need O(n^2) Memory link was in the index data but not checked against the bibliography; the reverse link (that paper citing FlashAttention) exists in the index, probably from a revised version, and is left out of the citation list.
The Lean Attention quote describes the problem rather than its partitioning method; the full text was not read.

Possibly relevant but not checked: activation recomputation and sequence parallelism in Megatron (Korthikanti et al. 2022, arXiv 2205.05198), Fully Pipelined Distributed Transformer, WallFacer, StarTrail, TASP, HyDra/FCP, MagiAttention, and kernels for non-NVIDIA hardware (AMD, TPU Pallas, Ascend).
No benchmarks or results figures were read; speedup claims come from abstracts only.

answer.summary:
I found 25 papers in four groups. All quotes come from scholarly-index or arXiv abstracts. Every citation link comes from Citation Lens reference-list data.

1. **Memory algorithms.** The online-softmax normalizer (Milakov & Gimelshein, 2018) and chunked attention (Rabe & Staats, 2021) show that exact attention needs only sub-quadratic memory. FlashAttention (2022) then made this fast by tiling for the GPU's on-chip SRAM, i.e. making the kernel I/O-aware. Blockwise Parallel Transformer (BPT) applies the same blockwise idea to the feedforward network as well.

2. **Single-GPU kernels and work partitioning.** The FlashAttention series follows each GPU generation:
   - FlashAttention-2 improves work partitioning across thread blocks and warps.
   - FlashAttention-3 (Hopper) uses warp specialization and asynchronous data movement.
   - FlashAttention-4 (2026, Blackwell) redesigns the pipeline because tensor cores have outgrown shared-memory bandwidth and exponential units.
   - Lean Attention changes how decode-phase work is split across compute units.
   - FlexAttention (compiler-generated kernels) and FlashMask (masks) extend fused exact kernels to more attention variants.

3. **Distributed exact attention.** Two families exist:
   - Ring/context parallelism passes KV blocks between devices: Sequence Parallelism (Li et al.), Ring Attention, DistFlashAttn, Striped Attention, BurstAttention, TokenRing, and Context Parallelism for million-token inference.
   - Head-parallel all-to-all: DeepSpeed-Ulysses, which cannot scale past the number of attention heads.
   - USP and LoongTrain combine the two. Megatron's sequence parallelism (Reducing Activation Recomputation) is the baseline both families build on.

4. **Recent distributed work (2024–2026).** The focus has shifted to communication and memory:
   - Mesh-Attention and ATTENTION2D tile the query × KV interaction in 2D for lower communication.
   - Tree Attention uses tree reductions for cross-device decoding.
   - Untied Ulysses splits attention by head to cut activation memory.

**Main trade-offs.** Ring methods overlap communication with compute but send traffic proportional to sequence length; Ulysses needs less communication but cannot use more devices than there are attention heads. 2D, tree and hybrid schemes trade between the two, and causal masking needs load balancing (striping, zig-zag).

**Exclusions (out of scope, not listed):**
- Approximate attention: sparse, low-rank or linear (e.g. Performer, Linformer, Reformer, MInference, linear-attention sequence parallelism such as LASP/ZeCO).
- Low-precision kernels (SageAttention, the FP8 path of FlashAttention-3).
- Serving and KV-cache policies (PagedAttention, StreamingLLM, KV eviction, LoongServe).

answer.summary:
The field breaks into four layers.

1. **Foundational algorithms.** Online softmax (Milakov & Gimelshein, 2018) and chunked lazy-softmax attention (Rabe & Staats, 2021) show that exact attention needs only sub-quadratic memory. Gradient checkpointing (Chen et al., 2016) adds the trade of recomputation for memory.

2. **GPU I/O-aware kernels.** FlashAttention (2022) turned these ideas into an SRAM-tiled, HBM-optimal fused kernel with backward-pass recomputation. FlashAttention-2 (2023) improved parallelism over sequence length and warp work partitioning. FA-3 (2024, Hopper) and FA-4 (2026, Blackwell) chase new hardware: asynchrony, warp specialization, exponential emulation and conditional rescaling. FlexAttention, ThunderKittens and FlashInfer (2024–25) generalize the kernel through compilers, tile DSLs and JIT templates. FlashBoB (Sept 2026) extends I/O-aware exactness to the double backward pass.

3. **Work partitioning for decode.** Lean Attention (and Flash-Decoding-style split-KV) uses the fact that the softmax merge is associative to balance work across SMs.

4. **Distributed exact attention.** Ring-style methods (Li et al. 2021 → BPT/Ring Attention → Striped, DistFlashAttn, context parallelism for inference) pass KV blocks point-to-point and overlap communication with compute. Load balancing under causal masks is the main problem. Ulysses uses all-to-all head sharding instead: communication is cheaper, but parallelism is capped by the number of heads. USP and LoongTrain hybridize the two. Tree Attention replaces the ring with tree reductions. MagiAttention (in the MAGI-1 paper) targets heterogeneous masks, and Untied Ulysses (2026) reduces CP activation memory with headwise chunking. The 2025 Long-Context Attention Benchmark compares kernels and CP methods side by side.

**Trade-offs.**
- Kernels trade portability for peak FLOP utilization.
- Ring methods scale to any number of devices but need overlap and load balancing.
- All-to-all methods are communication-efficient but limited by head count.

**Citation links** are drawn from well-established reference lists (e.g., FA cites Rabe & Staats and Milakov; Ring cites BPT) and from bibliography evidence seen in search (FlashBoB → ThunderKittens/FlashInfer). They were not exhaustively verified with a citation tool.

**Sources consulted:** arxiv.org/abs/2603.05451, arxiv.org/abs/2609.24089, arxiv.org/abs/2412.05496, arxiv.org/abs/2602.21196, arxiv.org/abs/2505.13211, arxiv.org/abs/2510.17896, arxiv.org/abs/2411.01783, arxiv.org/pdf/2405.07719, github.com/SandAI-org/MagiAttention.
gaps: Excluded by design and not listed: approximate attention (sparse, low-rank, linear, e.g. Reformer/Performer/Linformer; sparse-attention load balancers like FVAttn), low-precision variants (SageAttention, FA-3's FP8 path), and serving KV-cache policies (PagedAttention/vLLM, eviction/compression such as H2O and StreamingLLM). FlashInfer is included only for its exact kernels.

FA-4's abstract page does not use the word 'exact'. Its exactness is inferred from the FlashAttention lineage, and its exponential emulation may differ numerically from standard exp. Untied Ulysses's exactness is likewise not stated on its abstract page.

MagiAttention has no standalone arXiv paper found; MAGI-1 is used as the citable proxy (a March 2026 write-up may exist).

Activation-memory work outside attention (e.g., Korthikanti et al. selective recomputation, Megatron sequence parallelism) was left out to stay within the 25-paper ceiling.

answer.summary:
This work falls into three groups.

**1. Single-device memory algorithms.** Milakov and Gimelshein's online softmax (2018) keeps a running max and sum so softmax needs only one pass. Rabe and Staats (2021) used it to show exact attention can be computed in chunks with O(1) or O(log n) memory. Blockwise Parallel Transformer (BPT) extended chunking to the fused feedforward layer.

**2. GPU kernels that reduce memory traffic.**
- FlashAttention (2022) applied tiling and recomputation so the n×n score matrix never goes to GPU main memory (HBM). Memory becomes linear and the result stays exact.
- FlashAttention-2 changed how work is divided: across the sequence, and among warps.
- FlashAttention-3 (Hopper) and FlashAttention-4 (Blackwell, 2026) adapt the pipeline to each GPU generation: asynchrony, warp specialization, emulated exponentials, tensor memory.
- FlexAttention and FlashMask (2024–25) keep the fused exact kernel but generalize the masks and score changes, skipping blocks that are fully masked out.
- Lean Attention partitions decode-time work along the sequence to keep the whole GPU busy.

**3. Distributed exact attention.** There are two basic families:
- Ring-style key/value passing: Li et al.'s Ring Self-Attention, then Ring Attention, BurstAttention and TokenRing.
- Head-sharded all-to-all: DeepSpeed-Ulysses. It balances work well but cannot use more devices than there are attention heads.

Hybrids combine the two: USP, and LoongTrain's 2D-Attention. Causal masks leave ring devices with uneven work; Striped Attention, DistFlashAttn, zig-zag reordering and FCP address this.

For inference:
- The 2024 context-parallelism paper (2411.01783) adds pass-KV and pass-Q exact ring variants.
- Tree Attention replaces the ring with a tree reduction for decoding and reports up to 8x faster cross-device decoding.

The 2025 Long-Context Attention Benchmark is the best side-by-side comparison of kernels and context-parallel methods.

**Overall:** kernels set the cost of each attention block. Distributed schemes trade communication volume (ring) against limits from the number of heads (Ulysses). Recent work focuses on new hardware, flexible masks and load balancing under irregular masks.

**Sources and evidence:** FlashAttention-4, FlexAttention, FlashMask, Tree Attention, 2411.01783, 2510.17896 and FCP were confirmed through searches or arXiv pages this session. The other papers, their quotes and all citation links come from prior knowledge, not reference lists opened here. Key pages: arxiv.org/abs/2603.05451, arxiv.org/abs/2412.05496, arxiv.org/abs/2510.17896, arxiv.org/abs/2605.08524, arxiv.org/abs/2408.04093, arxiv.org/abs/2411.01783, arxiv.org/abs/2410.01359.
gaps:
Excluded by request:
- Approximate or sparse attention (Reformer, Performer, linear attention, sliding-window or top-k sparse kernels).
- Low-precision variants (FP8 or INT8 attention, the FP8 path of FlashAttention-3, SageAttention).
- Serving KV-cache policies (PagedAttention/vLLM paging, eviction, compression, prefix caching). FlashInfer and FlashDecoding-style split-K decoding kernels were left out as borderline serving work.

MagiAttention (flexible-mask context parallelism) has no standalone arXiv paper that I could find; it is described only in the MAGI-1 report's appendix and in docs. ByteScale and WLB-LLM (2025 load-balanced context parallelism) were not verified within the tool budget.

FCP (2605.08524): the abstract does not say whether attention stays exact. Abstracts for FlashAttention-4, USP, TokenRing, BurstAttention and Lean Attention were not quoted verbatim, so those quote fields are empty.
The citation links are inferred from prior knowledge of these papers' reference lists, not from reference lists checked in this session.

Little published work compares distributed exact attention on non-NVIDIA hardware (AMD, TPU, Trainium), handles the backward pass for decode-time tree reductions, or analyzes memory and communication theory jointly for hybrid head/context parallelism.
Recent exact-attention kernels for multi-head latent attention (MLA) or grouped-query attention (GQA), and ThunderKittens-style kernel DSLs, were not covered within the tool budget.

answer.summary:
**Lineage.** LoRA (2021) brings together two strands of earlier work:
- **Parameter-efficient transfer with a frozen backbone:** Houlsby adapters, prefix-tuning and prompt tuning.
- **The intrinsic-dimension view:** Li et al. 2018 and Aghajanyan et al. 2020 showed that fine-tuning works inside very low-dimensional subspaces. LoRA turns this into a low-rank update that can be merged into the weights, so it adds no inference latency, which adapters do.

The reference lists confirm LoRA cites all five of these foundation papers.

**Follow-ups.**
- **Memory-efficient:** QLoRA uses a 4-bit frozen base model and is by far the most-cited follow-up. LoRA-FA freezes A. GaLore moves the low-rank structure from the weights to the gradients, so all parameters can still be learned.
- **Reparameterized or structured:** AdaLoRA (SVD form with adaptive rank), DoRA (magnitude/direction split), VeRA (shared random matrices, close to the random-subspace idea), MoRA and RandLoRA (high- or full-rank updates on the same parameter budget).
- **Optimization and initialization fixes:** LoRA+ (separate learning rates for A and B), rsLoRA (1/sqrt(r) scaling), PiSSA (initialize from principal singular vectors), LoRA-GA (gradient-aligned initialization), EVA (initialize from activation variance).

**LoRA vs full fine-tuning analyses.**
- LoRA Learns Less and Forgets Less (2024) finds that full fine-tuning learns updates 10–100x higher in rank, while LoRA forgets less of the base model's abilities.
- The Illusion of Equivalence paper (NeurIPS 2024) finds structurally different solutions ('intruder dimensions') even when accuracy matches.

**2025–26.** Recent work tries to make LoRA behave like full fine-tuning:
- LoRA-One: theory linking adapters to the one-step full gradient.
- LoFT: projects Adam's optimizer moments into the low-rank subspace.
- CG-LoRA (2026): matches full fine-tuning's predictions using curvature.
- Zindari et al. (2026): theory showing LoRA can beat full fine-tuning when the gap between pretraining and the downstream task is effectively low-rank.

**Overall pattern.** Initialization and optimizer methods (PiSSA, LoRA-GA, LoRA-One, LoFT) close the convergence gap cheaply. High- or full-rank reparameterizations (MoRA, RandLoRA) target tasks that need a lot of capacity. The analyses suggest LoRA's lower rank is both why it forgets less and why it falls short on some tasks.

answer.summary:
I found 25 papers. The citation links come from reference-list evidence in Citation Lens; links I couldn't confirm are left out.

**Where LoRA comes from (2017–2021).** LoRA (2021) brings together two earlier lines of work:
- **Intrinsic dimensionality:** Li et al. (2018) and Aghajanyan et al. (2020) showed that fine-tuning can work in a very low-dimensional subspace. This is the basis for LoRA's assumption that the weight update is low-rank.
- **Parameter-efficient transfer:** Houlsby adapters (2019), prefix-tuning and prompt tuning (2021) trained only a small number of added parameters. LoRA's selling point against them is that its update merges back into the weights, so it adds no inference latency.

All of these links come from LoRA's own bibliography.

**Influential follow-ups (2023–24).** They fall into four groups:
- **Memory efficiency:** QLoRA (4-bit NF4 base plus LoRA; by far the most-cited follow-up), QA-LoRA, LoRA-FA, and GaLore. GaLore projects the gradients instead of constraining the weights, so it keeps full-parameter learning.
- **Reparameterization:** AdaLoRA (SVD form with rank pruning), DoRA (magnitude/direction split), MoRA (high-rank square update) and VeRA (shared random matrices with trained scaling vectors).
- **Optimization:** LoRA+ uses different learning rates for A and B.
- **Initialization:** PiSSA, LoRA-GA and EVA initialize the adapters from SVD, gradients or activations. Most of these papers say they are trying to close LoRA's convergence or accuracy gap with full fine-tuning.

**Recent work (2024-10 to 2026).** It splits into two strands:
- **Closing the gap to full fine-tuning:** LoRA-SB, RandLoRA (full-rank updates from random bases), GoRA (rank and initialization chosen from gradients) and LoRI (multi-task interference).
- **LoRA vs full fine-tuning analyses:**
  - "LoRA Learns Less and Forgets Less" (2024) found LoRA underperforms full fine-tuning but forgets less, while full fine-tuning learns updates of 10–100× higher rank.
  - "Illusion of Equivalence" (NeurIPS 2025) traces LoRA's forgetting to "intruder dimensions" in the trained weights.
  - "Optimizer-Model Consistency" (2026) argues that full fine-tuning with the pretraining optimizer forgets less than LoRA, which challenges the earlier "LoRA forgets less" finding.

**Not in the list:** Thinking Machines' "LoRA Without Regret" (Sept 2025) reports that rank-1 LoRA matches full fine-tuning in policy-gradient RL and that the best LoRA learning rate is about 10× the full fine-tuning rate. It is a blog post, not a paper, and I only saw it through third-party summaries, so I left it out.

Overall, LoRA roughly matches full fine-tuning in low-information settings such as RL and small supervised fine-tuning. Its rank limit shows up in continued pretraining and heavy supervised fine-tuning, which is what high-rank and full-rank variants like MoRA and RandLoRA target. The trade-off between learning and forgetting is still disputed.

answer.summary:
**Roots.** LoRA (2021) combines two earlier lines of work:
- **Intrinsic dimensionality.** Li et al. 2018 trained networks in random subspaces. Aghajanyan et al. 2020 showed that fine-tuning pretrained language models works in a very low-dimensional reparameterization.
- **Parameter-efficient transfer.** Adapters (Houlsby 2019) and prefix-tuning (2021) are the baselines LoRA beats on inference latency and ease of optimization.

He et al. (2021) then showed that adapters, prefix-tuning and LoRA are variants of one framework.

**Follow-ups fall into four groups:**
- **Memory efficiency.** QLoRA (a 4-bit quantized base) and LoftQ (initialization that accounts for quantization) shrink the frozen model. GaLore moves the low-rank idea to gradients and optimizer states, so all parameters are still trained.
- **Reparameterization and capacity.** AdaLoRA (adaptive rank via SVD), VeRA (shared random matrices plus trainable vectors, close to the random-subspace origins), DoRA (magnitude/direction split) and HiRA (a Hadamard product that gives high-rank updates).
- **Optimization dynamics.** LoRA+ (different learning rates for A and B) and rsLoRA (1/√r scaling).
- **Initialization that imitates full fine-tuning.** PiSSA → LoRA-GA → LoRA-One / LoRA-SB. These start the adapters in the subspace of the weights or of the full fine-tuning gradient.

**Comparisons with full fine-tuning.** The analyses do not converge on a single answer:
- Biderman et al. 2024: LoRA learns less on the target task but forgets less of what the base model knew.
- Shuttleworth et al. (2024/25): even at equal accuracy, LoRA's solutions are structurally different from full fine-tuning (intruder dimensions).
- 2026 theory (Zindari et al.): LoRA can generalize better than full fine-tuning when the task shift is effectively low-rank.
- MoLF (2026): which method wins depends on the task, so it routes between dense and low-rank updates.

**Recent re-evaluations.** Two 2026 benchmark papers (Learning Rate Matters; the unified LoRAFactory study) report that once learning rates are tuned properly, vanilla LoRA matches most variants (within about 1–2%). This puts many claimed gains from variants in doubt.

papers.quote: we empirically show that common pre-trained models have a very low intrinsic dimension

papers.title: Parameter-Efficient Transfer Learning for NLP
papers.reason: Original bottleneck adapters. LoRA is positioned against them, matching quality without adding inference latency.
papers.quote: Adapter modules yield a compact and extensible model; they add only a few trainable parameters per task

papers.title: Prefix-Tuning: Optimizing Continuous Prompts for Generation
papers.reason: A frozen-LM continuous-prefix method. It is a main baseline in LoRA's experiments.
papers.quote: keeps language model parameters frozen, but optimizes a small continuous task-specific vector (called the prefix)

papers.title: The Power of Scale for Parameter-Efficient Prompt Tuning
papers.reason: Soft prompt tuning. LoRA cites it as a prompt-based alternative.
papers.quote: a simple yet effective mechanism for learning "soft prompts" to condition frozen language models to perform specific downstream tasks

papers.title: Towards a Unified View of Parameter-Efficient Transfer Learning
papers.reason: Puts adapters, prefix tuning and LoRA in one framework of modifications to hidden states.
papers.quote: present a unified framework that establishes connections between them

papers.title: QLoRA: Efficient Finetuning of Quantized LLMs
papers.reason: Combines a 4-bit NF4-quantized frozen base with LoRA adapters, making 65B fine-tuning possible on one GPU.
papers.quote: reduces memory usage enough to finetune a 65B parameter model on a single 48GB GPU while preserving full 16-bit finetuning task performance

papers.title: DoRA: Weight-Decomposed Low-Rank Adaptation
papers.reason: Splits weights into magnitude and direction and applies LoRA to direction only, narrowing the gap to full fine-tuning.
papers.quote: decomposes the pre-trained weight into two components, magnitude and direction, for fine-tuning, specifically employing LoRA for directional updates

papers.title: AdaLoRA: Adaptive Budget Allocation for Parameter-Efficient Fine-Tuning
papers.reason: Uses an SVD-style parameterization with importance-based rank pruning across layers.
papers.quote: adaptively allocates the parameter budget among weight matrices according to their importance score

papers.title: VeRA: Vector-based Random Matrix Adaptation
papers.reason: Shares frozen random low-rank matrices across layers and trains only scaling vectors, combining random-subspace ideas from the intrinsic-dimension work with LoRA.
papers.quote: significantly reduces the number of trainable parameters compared to LoRA, yet maintains the same performance

papers.title: LoftQ: LoRA-Fine-Tuning-Aware Quantization for Large Language Models
papers.reason: Quantizes jointly with LoRA initialization to reduce the quantization gap in QLoRA-style training.
papers.quote: simultaneously quantizes an LLM and finds a proper low-rank initialization for LoRA fine-tuning

papers.title: PiSSA: Principal Singular Values and Singular Vectors Adaptation of Large Language Models
papers.reason: Initializes adapters from the principal singular components and freezes the residual. It started the line of initialization-based variants.
papers.quote: initializes the adaptor matrices A and B with the principal components of the original matrix W, and put the remaining components into a residual matrix

papers.title: GaLore: Memory-Efficient LLM Training by Gradient Low-Rank Projection
papers.reason: Moves the low-rank idea from weights to gradients and optimizer states, allowing full-parameter learning with less memory than LoRA.
papers.quote: a training strategy that allows full-parameter learning but is more memory-efficient than common low-rank adaptation methods such as LoRA

papers.title: LoRA+: Efficient Low Rank Adaptation of Large Models
papers.reason: Shows that LoRA is suboptimal at large width and fixes this with different learning rates for A and B.
papers.quote: Low Rank Adaptation (LoRA) as originally introduced in Hu et al. (2021) leads to suboptimal finetuning of models with large width

papers.title: LoRA Learns Less and Forgets Less
papers.reason: Large-scale code and math study: LoRA underperforms full fine-tuning on the target domain but forgets less outside it.
papers.quote: LoRA better maintains the base model's performance on tasks outside the target domain

papers.title: LoRA vs Full Fine-tuning: An Illusion of Equivalence
papers.reason: Finds that LoRA introduces 'intruder dimensions' (new high-ranking singular vectors) that full fine-tuning does not, linked to forgetting and weaker continual learning.
papers.quote: new, high-ranking singular vectors

papers.title: MiLoRA: Harnessing Minor Singular Components for Parameter-Efficient LLM Finetuning
papers.reason: Adapts the minor rather than the principal singular components to preserve pre-trained knowledge.
papers.quote: only updates the minor singular components of weight matrices while keeping the principle singular components frozen

papers.title: LoRA-GA: Low-Rank Adaptation with Gradient Approximation
papers.reason: Initializes LoRA so its first-step update matches the full fine-tuning gradient, which speeds convergence.
papers.quote: aligns the gradients of low-rank matrix product with those of full fine-tuning at the first step

papers.title: LoRA-Pro: Are Low-Rank Adapters Properly Optimized?
papers.reason: Adjusts LoRA's A and B gradients so the low-rank update approximates the full fine-tuning gradient during training, not just at initialization.

papers.title: LoRA-One: One-Step Full Gradient Could Suffice for Fine-Tuning Large Language Models, Provably and Efficiently
papers.reason: Proves that LoRA aligns with singular subspaces of the one-step full gradient and initializes from them, with convergence and generalization guarantees.
papers.quote: theory-driven algorithm, LoRA-One, where the linear convergence (as well as generalization) is built

papers.title: A Unified Study of LoRA Variants: Taxonomy, Review, Codebase, and Empirical Evaluation
papers.reason: Groups variants along four axes (rank, dynamics, initialization, MoE). Finds variants are very sensitive to learning rate and that well-tuned vanilla LoRA matches or beats most of them.

papers.title: LoRA vs. Full Fine-Tuning: A Theoretical Perspective
papers.reason: A linear-regression excess-risk analysis identifying regimes where LoRA beats full fine-tuning, especially when the task gap is effectively low-rank or noise is high.

papers.title: Beyond LoRA vs. Full Fine-Tuning: Gradient-Guided Optimizer Routing for LLM Adaptation
papers.reason: Shows that which method wins depends on the task, and proposes MoLF, which routes between full fine-tuning and LoRA update pathways.

papers.title: TaRA: Training-Aware Low-Rank Adaptation Initialization
papers.reason: Uses activation and gradient covariance to initialize LoRA so it approximates the full-rank gradient. Reported to beat PiSSA, CorDA and LoRA-One.
papers.quote: initializes LoRA such that the gradients induced by the low-rank factors closely approximate the gradient of the corresponding full-rank weight matrix

answer.summary:
LoRA joins two earlier lines of work. One is parameter-efficient transfer: adapters (Houlsby 2019), prefix-tuning and prompt tuning. The other is intrinsic-dimensionality work (Li 2018; Aghajanyan 2020), which shows fine-tuning can happen in tiny subspaces. LoRA's key addition is a low-rank update that can be merged back into the weights, so inference has no added latency. He et al. (2021) then placed LoRA in a unified framework alongside the other PEFT methods.

Follow-ups fall into four groups:
(1) Memory efficiency: QLoRA and LoftQ quantize the frozen base. GaLore moves the low-rank projection onto gradients and optimizer states, allowing full-rank learning.
(2) Reparameterization and parameter budget: AdaLoRA allocates rank adaptively, VeRA uses shared random matrices plus trained scaling vectors, and DoRA separates magnitude from direction.
(3) Initialization and optimization: PiSSA and MiLoRA build on SVD, while LoRA-GA, LoRA-Pro, LoRA-One (ICML 2025) and TaRA (2026) build on gradient alignment. LoRA+ uses different learning rates for A and B. The common trend is to make LoRA's training dynamics imitate full fine-tuning.
(4) Analyses of LoRA versus full fine-tuning: Biderman et al. (2024) find LoRA "learns less and forgets less". Shuttleworth et al. (2024/25) trace the difference to spectral "intruder dimensions". A 2026 linear-regression theory paper (Zindari et al.) identifies regimes where LoRA generalizes better than full fine-tuning. MoLF (2026) routes between the two methods per task. The January 2026 unified benchmark tempers the variant race: once learning rates are tuned properly, vanilla LoRA matches or beats most variants.

How the citation links were sourced: the edges into the 2024–26 papers come from what the retrieved pages and snippets said about each paper's comparisons and related work. The edges among the older papers rely on well-known reference lists and were not re-checked in this session.
gaps: I could not get verbatim abstract text for the 2026 papers (2601.22708, 2605.19018, 2605.07111) or for LoRA-Pro, so their quote fields are left empty. Several older quotes come from memory of the abstracts and should be checked against the arXiv pages.

With an 8-call budget, most citation edges were not checked against reference lists. The edges for older papers (for example DoRA→VeRA, PiSSA→LoftQ, VeRA→Aghajanyan) rely on known bibliographies. For TaRA→PiSSA/LoRA-One, the evidence is the baselines it reports.
Thinking Machines' 'LoRA Without Regret' (Sep 2025), a widely discussed practitioner analysis, is a blog post rather than an arXiv paper, so it is not listed.
Not covered: ReLoRA, rsLoRA, CorDA, EVA, HiRA, LoRA-SB, MoE-LoRA (e.g., MoLoRA/HydraLoRA), and LoRA for RL/RLHF and diffusion models.
The 2026 preprints (theory paper, MoLF, TaRA) are recent and not peer-reviewed. Their influence cannot be judged yet.
